how_to_read: The 7-day notice skill's stories, in the repair stories' shape. Each runs on lease_rules.txt in this folder: comparisons/skills/lease.txt with a new clause 11 on pets, guests, parking, and noise. 'today' is the date count_days compares with. 'facts' are confirmed facts. 'points' are what a right answer must convey, judged by meaning; a point written wholly in parentheses is helpful detail, not required. 'mistakes' make an answer wrong. 'law' quotes the statute word for word; 'dates' are the count_days results the answer needs. 'open': true marks a key waiting on the author (notice-6, AUTHOR.md item 22), not counted as settled. Every story holds school_housing. Check with: python ../skills/check_key.py notice_received_violation/stories.json (from comparisons/each_skill/).

Demand is hereby made that you remedy the noncompliance within 7 days of receipt of this notice or your lease shall be deemed terminated and you shall vacate the premises upon such termination. If this same conduct or conduct of a similar nature is repeated within 12 months, your tenancy is subject to termination without further warning and without your being given an opportunity to cure the noncompliance.

stories.message: I got a letter from the office about my dog. It's dated March 2 but the manager handed it to me March 9. It says I have 7 days to fix it or my lease is over. Do I have to move out? How long do I have?
stories.answer: You do not have to move out if you fix this in time. The 7 days run from the day the letter was handed to you, not the date on it, so your last day is March 16. Fixing it means the dog is out of the apartment, or you have your landlord's written consent, as clause 11 says. If you fix it in time, your landlord may not end the lease on this notice. If the dog comes back within 12 months, your landlord can file an eviction case without another notice. Even if the 7 days pass, your landlord has to go to court to get the apartment back, and cannot lock you out.
points: Says the tenant does not have to move out if the problem is fixed in time: this notice gives 7 days to fix it, and if it is fixed the landlord may not end the lease on it.
Gives the last day as 2026-03-16, from count_days, counted from the day it was delivered, not the date on the letter.
Says what fixing it means under clause 11: the dog is out, or the landlord gives written consent.
Says that if it happens again within 12 months, the landlord may bring an eviction case without another notice.
Says the notice does not by itself put the tenant out: the landlord needs a court case. (The landlord may not lock them out.)
mistakes: Counts the 7 days from the date on the letter (2026-03-09).
Says the tenant must leave within 7 days whatever they do.
Says that fixing it ends the matter for good, leaving out the next 12 months.

Gives a date it worked out itself instead of from count_days.
Says how long something has lasted, or how long until a date, from its own counting (repeating the tenant's own words is not this mistake).

stories.message: I got a letter saying my lease is terminated and I have 7 days to get out because my boyfriend stayed over too many nights. I never got a warning before this. He's gone now. Do I really have to be out in 7 days?
stories.answer: Not by the notice alone. Your landlord has to file a court case to get the apartment back, and cannot lock you out. An unauthorized guest is on the statute's list of things a tenant should get the chance to fix, and you had no earlier written warning, so a notice ending the lease at once does not fit; you should have had 7 days to fix it. Still, do not ignore the notice. The 7 days end April 13, and after that your landlord can sue. You could raise the wrong kind of notice in court, and whether it ends the case is for the court. The statute lets a landlord fix a flawed notice in some cases, and whether that reaches this kind of case is not settled.

stories.message: One party, one noise complaint, and now I have a letter saying my lease is terminated and I've got 7 days to leave. Can they do that over one party? They've never warned me about anything.
stories.answer: The law does not settle whether your landlord can do that over one party. The statute's list of things a tenant gets no chance to fix names a 'subsequent or continued' disturbance, and this was a first one. Noise is not on its list of things a tenant may fix either, and both lists are only examples. One reading: this is the kind a tenant should get to fix, so the notice should have given you 7 days. The other: the lists are only examples, so your landlord may treat it as the kind with no chance to fix. Either way the notice does not put you out by itself: your landlord needs a court case. The 7 days end May 11, and after that your landlord can sue.
points: Opens by saying it is not settled whether the landlord can end the lease this way, and leans neither way. Gives the reason: the no-fix list names a 'subsequent or continued' disturbance, this was a first complaint, noise is not on the fix list, and both lists are only examples.
Gives both readings and what each means for the tenant.

('Material' is not defined, and an answer may raise it with both readings. If sued, the tenant must meet 83.60(2).)

stories.message: I got a warning letter in January about noise, then we had another loud party last weekend, and now I got a letter saying my lease is terminated and I've got 7 days. Can I just promise no more parties and fix it? Do I get another chance?
stories.answer: No, the law does not give you another chance under this kind of notice. A repeat of a similar violation within 12 months of a written warning is one the statute lets a landlord end without a chance to fix. Your warning is dated January 15, its 12 months run to about January 15, 2027, and the party on March 20 falls inside them. You may still ask your landlord to let it go, but your landlord does not have to. The notice does not put you out by itself: your landlord needs a court case. The 7 days end March 30, and after that your landlord can sue.

stories.message: I got a notice March 20 saying my lease was terminated because of a fight my guests had in the hallway on March 14. I paid April rent through the portal anyway on April 1 and they took it. Nothing has happened since. Does that change anything?
stories.answer: Yes. A landlord who takes rent knowing about a violation gives up the right to end the lease or sue over that violation. Your landlord knew about the fight, since it sent the notice, and took all of April's rent after that. It has not happened again. So your landlord gave up ending the lease over that fight. That does not cover anything new. There is nothing you need to do now; you would raise this if your landlord sues.

stories.message: The manager texted me that my car has been in the visitor spot and I have 7 days to move it or my lease is terminated. Is a text even a legal notice? Do I have to do anything?
stories.answer: The law does not settle whether a text counts. It names mailing, handing over a copy, e-mail under a signed agreement, and leaving a copy at the home if you are away. A text is none of these, and your lease says you and your landlord did not agree to e-mail. One reading: this is not the required notice, so no count has started. The other: a notice that actually reached you is enough. Moving the car to your own space by February 23 meets both readings. Either way the text does not put you out by itself: your landlord needs a court case.

stories.message: The landlord filed an eviction against me over that notice and I got served yesterday. The damage wasn't me. What do I do?
stories.answer: Act on the court papers first. To defend the case you must meet a rule about the court registry, an account the court clerk keeps. You pay in the rent the complaint claims and the rent that comes due while the case goes on, or you file a motion asking the court to set the amount, within 5 days after you were served, not counting Saturdays, Sundays, and legal holidays. The summons states this. This tool does not count those days. If you miss it, you lose your defenses other than payment, and the court must order you removed. If you meet it, you can raise that you did not do the damage. Other court steps are outside this tool.
points: Leads with what the tenant must do to defend: pay into the court registry the rent as the complaint alleges and the rent coming due during the case, or file a motion to determine the amount, within 5 days excluding Saturdays, Sundays, and legal holidays after service; the summons states the requirement (83.56(5)(b), 83.60(2)).
Says what follows if they miss it: an absolute waiver of defenses other than payment, and a default judgment for removal.
Says the tenant can raise that they did not do it as a defense once that rule is met.
(83.56(2)(a)'s example turns on damage 'by intentional act'. Other court steps are outside the tool. An answer may say to get a lawyer at once.)

Says the tenant can simply tell the court they did not do it, leaving out the registry rule.

stories.message: I got a lease termination letter this morning over a door I damaged. I'm not going to fight it. If I move out by June 8, am I done? Do I still owe rent through July? What about my deposit?
stories.answer: Moving out does not by itself settle what you owe, and the law does not settle whether you still owe rent through July. One reading: your landlord ended the lease, and that is the choice that ends any further liability. The other: the rule on remedies covers any tenant who broke the lease and gave up the home, so your landlord keeps its choice, including holding you to the rent. Your landlord must also follow the deposit rules, and may make a claim for the door. To keep the landlord's duty to send you a notice about the deposit, give a written notice by hand or certified mail with your new address; for a June 8 move, the last day is today.
points: Opens by saying moving out does not by itself settle what is owed, and that whether the tenant still owes rent through July is not settled. Gives both readings (83.595(1) against 83.595's opening) and leans neither way.
Says the landlord must comply with 83.49(3) for the deposit (83.56(6)), and may make a claim on it through those steps.

Gives the 7-day notice before leaving: written, by hand or certified mail, with an address; the last day for a June 8 move is 2026-06-01, today, from count_days. Says what it does: it keeps the landlord's duty to send a notice about the deposit.
(The last day to leave under the notice is 2026-06-08, from count_days.)
